meta.title: Who really said "To one who has faith, no explanation is necessary. To one without faith, no explanation is possible"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. This aphorism is not from Thomas Aquinas — it appears in no work of his. It is an anonymous saying (documented by 1882) popularized by the 1943 film The Song of Bernadette.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To one who has faith, no explanation is necessary. To one without faith, no explanation is possible'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aquinas. An anonymous aphorism (documented by 1882) made famous by the 1943 film The Song of Bernadette; its wording appears in no Aquinas text.

answer.label: Not Thomas Aquinas — an anonymous aphorism
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in no work of Thomas Aquinas and is absent from Wikiquote’s Aquinas page. The saying is fundamentally anonymous — the earliest known instance is an 1882 St. Louis Post-Dispatch editorial (“No explanation is needed for a believer; no explanation suffices for an unbeliever”) — and its famous modern form is the prologue of the 1943 film ‘The Song of Bernadette,’ written by screenwriter George Seaton. The Aquinas credit is a later, unsupported misattribution.

source.excerpt: For those who believe in God, no explanation is necessary. For those who do not believe in God, no explanation is possible.
trail: Earliest documented form: an 1882 St. Louis Post-Dispatch editorial — “No explanation is needed for a believer; no explanation suffices for an unbeliever” — with no author named, per Quote Investigator.
The famous modern wording is the on-screen prologue of the 1943 film, written by George Seaton: “For those who believe in God, no explanation is necessary…” — transcribed in the AFI Catalog.
The line is not attested for Thomas Aquinas — it appears nowhere on his Wikiquote page, and even the Werfel credit is filed under “Disputed” on Wikiquote’s Werfel page.
source.excerptNote: The verbatim on-screen prologue of the 1943 film ‘The Song of Bernadette’ (screenplay by George Seaton), as transcribed by the AFI Catalog. The Aquinas-credited version simply swaps “believe in God” for “has faith” / “without faith.”

source.rightsNote: This exact English wording (“To one who has faith… To one without faith…”) is an anonymous modern variant with no identifiable author or first-publication record. The underlying aphorism’s 1882 form is old enough to be public-domain, but that is different wording; the widely quoted 1943 film prologue is a distinct, identifiable variant (George Seaton / Twentieth Century-Fox). Because the origin of this specific phrasing cannot be pinned down, we assert no copyright status.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: Where the saying actually comes from
author.metaLine: Aphorism documented by 1882 · popularized by the 1943 film The Song of Bernadette
author.bio: This saying about faith and explanation has no single documented author. Its earliest known appearance is an anonymous 1882 St. Louis Post-Dispatch editorial; over the decades it was variously claimed by or credited to Father John LaFarge, Bishop Charles Brent, and others, and also floated as a line of Ignatius of Loyola. Its best-known modern form is the on-screen prologue of the 1943 film The Song of Bernadette, adapted from Franz Werfel’s novel by screenwriter George Seaton — though the phrase does not actually appear in Werfel’s book. The attribution to Thomas Aquinas is a still later, unsupported reassignment.

misattribution.heading: A quote with many claimants — but not Aquinas
misattribution.intro: This is a genuinely wandering aphorism. It has been pinned on several people over 140 years; Thomas Aquinas is one of the least supported of them.

items.why: The line appears in no work of Aquinas and is absent from his Wikiquote page entirely. Aquinas did write about faith and reason, but this modern one-liner is not a translation or paraphrase of any identified passage of his.

items.who: Franz Werfel / The Song of Bernadette
items.why: The wording most people know is the 1943 film’s prologue, written by screenwriter George Seaton; Quote Investigator checked Werfel’s 1942 novel and found the saying is not in it.

items.who: Father John LaFarge, Bishop Charles Brent, Ignatius of Loyola
items.why: LaFarge claimed authorship in his 1954 memoir and the line was credited to Bishop Brent as early as 1940; it is also loosely attached to Ignatius of Loyola on Wikiquote. None predate the anonymous 1882 printing.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: an anonymous aphorism documented by 1882 and made famous by the 1943 film The Song of Bernadette — not Thomas Aquinas.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Aquinas
lead: The aphorism’s neat chiasmus — belief needs no proof, unbelief accepts none — reads like medieval scholastic theology, so it drifts naturally toward the most famous theologian of faith-and-reason. But its documented life is modern and popular, not scholastic: a newspaper editorial, a bestselling novel about Lourdes, and above all a much-loved 1943 film whose very first words are this line.

Because the film presented the sentence with no author, it became free-floating — and quote sites in the internet era supplied a prestigious name. Aquinas, Werfel, LaFarge, Brent and Ignatius have all been offered; the only defensible answer is that no one can be shown to have coined it.
detailsBody: 1882 — St. Louis Post-Dispatch prints the earliest known form, anonymously.
1940 — a private publication credits Bishop Charles Brent; 1943 — the film ‘The Song of Bernadette’ opens with the saying, unattributed.
1954 — Father John LaFarge claims authorship in his memoir; the Aquinas credit is a still-later internet-era development.
context.pull: Belief needs no proof; unbelief accepts none — a line everyone quotes and no one can claim.
